title: Grow a Pair by Adding
statement:
You hold a pair of positive integers (x, y). In one move you may replace it with either (x + y, y) or (x, x + y): add one number into the other.

Starting from (sx, sy), return true if some sequence of zero or more moves reaches exactly (tx, ty), and false otherwise.

examples.why: The last move must have made 8 from 8 − 7 = 1, giving (1, 7). But x never shrinks, and 1 < 3.
Add x into y nine times. Jumping back with 13 % 1 = 0 would overshoot sy; once x matches, check that ty − sy is a multiple of x.

hints: Going forward branches into two choices at every step. Going backward from (tx, ty), how many choices are there?
Since both numbers are positive, the larger one must have been made last: (tx, ty) with tx > ty came from (tx − ty, ty). Walking back is a single path.
Subtracting ty over and over is just tx % ty. Stop the shortcut when one coordinate already matches the start, and finish with a divisibility check.

explain.intuition:
Forward, the moves branch. Backward they do not: in (tx, ty) with tx > ty, the last move must have added ty into x, because adding into y would have made y the bigger one. So there is exactly one way back, and you just follow it until you drop below the start.

Following it one subtraction at a time can take a billion steps, for example from (1, 1000000000). Repeated subtraction of ty from tx is tx % ty, the same speed-up as Euclid's GCD algorithm. The one catch: the modulo can jump past the start. When ty already equals sy, stop jumping and check whether tx − sx is a multiple of ty.
steps: While tx > sx and ty > sy and tx ≠ ty: if tx > ty set tx %= ty, otherwise ty %= tx.
If tx == sx: return ty > sy and (ty − sy) % tx == 0.
If ty == sy: return tx > sx and (tx − sx) % ty == 0.
pitfalls: Searching forward with BFS or recursion. The tree of pairs explodes, and values reach a billion.
Applying the modulo all the way down. With (1, 4) → (1, 13), 13 % 1 = 0 drops below sy and wrongly returns false.
Stepping back from tx == ty. A pair of equal numbers cannot be produced by a move, so only the start itself can be equal.

solutions.title: Walk back one subtraction at a time
solutions.idea: The larger coordinate was made last, so subtract the smaller from it until you reach the start or go below it.

solutions.title: Walk back with modulo
solutions.idea: Batch the repeated subtractions with %, like Euclid's algorithm, and finish with a divisibility check once one coordinate matches.

followups: Return the fewest moves needed instead of yes or no.
Allow the move (x − y, y) as well, when the result stays positive. Which pairs are reachable now? (Hint: gcd.)
